stem: A client with chronic heart failure asks what an appropriate nutrition plan generally emphasizes. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: Choose a heart-healthy pattern with vegetables, fruits, whole grains, healthy proteins, minimally processed foods, and lower-sodium choices, and follow any fluid limit prescribed by the health care team.
options.B: Use the same fixed sodium and fluid restriction for every person with heart failure, regardless of congestion, laboratory findings, other conditions, or the individualized treatment plan.
options.C: Focus mainly on calorie intake and body weight, because food quality and sodium choices do not meaningfully affect the nutrition plan once heart failure is established.
options.D: Replace minimally processed foods with more ultraprocessed foods when possible, because packaged foods make sodium intake more predictable and are preferred in heart-healthy dietary patterns.

rationale: The American Heart Association's 2026 dietary guidance describes a heart-healthy pattern emphasizing vegetables and fruits, whole grains, healthy protein sources, unsaturated fats, minimally processed foods, and reduced sodium. AHA heart-failure self-care guidance states that some clients may be advised to limit fluid and should ask the health care professional how much to drink. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart-failure guideline recommends avoiding excessive sodium for stage C heart failure but notes limited evidence for specific universal sodium thresholds and uncertain benefit of fluid restriction in advanced heart failure with hyponatremia. Therefore A correctly combines the general dietary pattern with individualized fluid guidance. B improperly universalizes restrictions, while C and D contradict current cardiovascular nutrition guidance.
educational_objective: Teach heart-failure nutrition as a heart-healthy dietary pattern with lower-sodium choices and individualized fluid guidance rather than applying one fixed sodium or fluid restriction to every client.
source_organization: American Heart Association (AHA); American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association/Heart Failure Society of America
source_document_title: 2026 Dietary Guidance to Improve Cardiovascular Health; Lifestyle Changes for Heart Failure; 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
source_version_date: AHA dietary guidance updated March 31, 2026; current AHA heart-failure self-care guidance accessed 2026-08-25; HF guideline published April 1, 2022
source_locator: AHA 2026 Dietary Guidance > Top Things to Know, item 7: heart-healthy dietary pattern includes vegetables/fruits, whole grains, healthy proteins, unsaturated fats, minimally processed foods, reduced added sugars and sodium. AHA Lifestyle Changes for Heart Failure > Track your daily fluid intake: the health care team may recommend limiting liquid intake; ask the health care professional how much liquid to drink each day. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF Guideline > Section 7.1.2 Dietary Sodium Restriction: avoiding excessive sodium is reasonable for stage C HF, while evidence for specific thresholds is low quality; Section 8.2: benefit of fluid restriction in advanced HF with hyponatremia is uncertain.
source_claim_supported: A heart-healthy dietary pattern emphasizes minimally processed, nutrient-dense foods and reduced sodium; heart-failure fluid limits are individualized rather than a universal fixed prescription for every client.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort > Nutrition and Oral Hydration, printed p. 37: consider client choices regarding nutritional requirements and dietary restrictions; monitor hydration status; evaluate nutritional status and intervene as needed; provide and maintain special diets based on diagnosis/nutritional needs, including low-sodium diets.
blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — individualized nutrition and fluid education in chronic heart failure
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four choices to remove the absolute-word cue and make the distractors realistic nutrition-plan errors. The corrected item preserves the heart-failure nutrition construct while using current 2026 AHA dietary guidance and explicitly avoiding an unsupported universal sodium or fluid prescription.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Chronic heart failure — nutrition and fluid self-management
audit_findings.stem: PASS — asks for a general nutrition emphasis without implying a universal numeric sodium or fluid target.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly reflects the 2026 heart-healthy dietary pattern and individualized heart-failure fluid guidance; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — sodium/fluid modification can be clinically appropriate, but one fixed prescription for every client overstates the evidence and ignores individual findings.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — energy balance matters, but current AHA guidance also explicitly addresses food quality and sodium.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — current AHA guidance favors minimally processed rather than ultraprocessed foods and reduced sodium.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only choice that combines current dietary-pattern guidance with individualized fluid management without unsupported universalization.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B overgeneralizes restrictions; C omits established dietary-quality guidance; D reverses the minimally processed-food recommendation.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — the keyed option is comparable in length and specificity to the alternatives and no keyed-only absolute wording remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Basic Care and Comfort directly includes dietary restrictions, hydration assessment, nutritional evaluation, and diagnosis-based special diets.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether B could be defended from traditional heart-failure teaching; the current HF guideline explicitly notes limited evidence for fixed sodium thresholds and uncertain fluid-restriction benefit in specified advanced-HF settings, so individualized guidance in A remains uniquely best.
